subject: Ragged negative binomial time series - how to speed up

messages.author: b5cbe02d295306d7
messages.subject: Ragged negative binomial time series - how to speed up
parts:
Hi Stan folks

I am new to Stan - & to Bayesian modelling - so I am not sure whether my slow model is badly written or 'thats-how-long-it-takes-given-the-number-of-parameters' (or of course both).

I have an unbalanced panel of around 350 time series.  The data are weekly counts of people receiving a social service.   The task - at this stage - is to separately identify the 'launch' effect of the service from the trend (which might be related to the economy, government policy etc).

So I am using a negative binomial with both a non-linear trend and a non-linear 'maturity' curve.  The model has fourier and xmas seasonality too.  

The good news is that the model runs, converges and predictive checks match the data reasonably.  But it takes 3 hours to run just 15 time series of about 240 observations each.  And I would like to add a bit more complexity & hierarchy to this model too (eg hierarchy to the NBD dispersion, predictors for the group effects etc).

The code is below & attached.   Very grateful for any help.



Enter code here...
data {
int<lower=1> N;                 // number of observations
int<lower=1> J;                 // number of groups
int<lower=1> K;                 // number of linear predictors
int<lower=1> j_start[J];        // start index for group_j
int<lower=1> j_end[J];          // end index for group_j
int<lower=1> fb_obs[J];         // panel size for each group
int<lower=1,upper=J> jj[N];     // groups index
int<lower=0> y_data[N];         // people served by unit
matrix[N,K] season;             // matrix of seasonals (fourier + xmas)
vector[N] age;                  // maturity age, time in weeks since opening

}

parameters{
  real intercept;      // common intercept to anchor the trends
  real<lower=0> phi;   // shape parameter for negative binomial

  vector[J] beta_maturity_0_raw; // groups models - individual intercepts
  real<lower=0.0> sigma_maturity_0; //
  real mu_maturity_0;
  real<lower=0,upper=1> beta_maturity_1; // pooled maturity impact by group's

  // seasonality (pooled)
  vector[K] beta_seasonal;
  real mu_seasonal;
  real sigma_seasonal;

  // time trend
  vector[N] date_deltas;  // should be (N-J)
  real<lower=0,upper=2> sigma_delta;
}

transformed parameters{
vector[J] beta_maturity_0; // different means per group
vector[N] beta_trend;      // evolving trend for each group

beta_maturity_0 <- mu_maturity_0 + sigma_maturity_0 * beta_maturity_0_raw;

// create trend variable in two steps.
  // 1. d(date_delta) ~ N(d(date_delta),data_sigma)
  // 2. correctly date align in matrix (real_delats) & cumulative sum
  {  vector[N] real_deltas;  // trend variables
      for(j in 1:J){
        real_deltas[j_start[j]] <- 0.0; // first row = zero ****
          for(t in j_start[j]:(j_end[j]-1))
            real_deltas[t+1] <- date_deltas[t];
        beta_trend[j_start[j]:j_end[j]] <- intercept +
          cumulative_sum(real_deltas[j_start[j]:j_end[j]]);
       }
  }

  }

 model{
  vector[N] y_hat; // latent variable
  vector[N] eta;   // linear predictor
  eta <-  season * beta_seasonal;

  // impact of 'maturity' of unit - nonlinear growth curve
  for (n in 1:N) {
    eta[n] <-  eta[n] + beta_maturity_0[jj[n]]*(exponential_cdf(
      age[n], beta_maturity_1));
  }

  // Priors
  phi ~ cauchy(10,5);
  beta_maturity_0_raw ~ normal(0,1);
  mu_maturity_0 ~ normal(0,5);
  sigma_maturity_0 ~ cauchy(0,5);
  beta_seasonal ~ normal(mu_seasonal,sigma_seasonal);
  mu_seasonal ~ normal(0,5);
  sigma_seasonal ~ cauchy(0,5);
  beta_maturity_1 ~ normal(0.4,0.3); // different maturity by group, scale
  sigma_delta ~ cauchy(0,0.2); // simple prior for 'smoothness'. not hierarchical

// model likelihood
  for(j in 1:J){

    // trend evolution
    date_deltas[j_start[j]] ~ normal(0,10); // first observation has looser prior
      for(t in (j_start[j]+1):(j_end[j]-1))
        date_deltas[t] ~ normal(date_deltas[t-1],sigma_delta);

    // latent 'state'
       y_hat[j_start[j]:j_end[j]] <-  eta[j_start[j]:j_end[j]] +
            beta_trend[j_start[j]:j_end[j]];

      increment_log_prob(neg_binomial_2_log_log(
        y_data[j_start[j]:j_end[j]],
        y_hat[j_start[j]:j_end[j]],
        phi));
              }
      }

 generated quantities{
    vector[N] y_predict;
    {
    vector[N] nu;
    vector[N] y_hat_predict;
    y_hat_predict <-  season * beta_seasonal;
       for (n in 1:N) {
         y_hat_predict[n] <- y_hat_predict[n] + beta_maturity_0[jj[n]]*(exponential_cdf(
           age[n], beta_maturity_1)) + beta_trend[n];
       }
    nu <- exp(y_hat_predict);

    // gets around the lack of stability with neg_binomial_2_log_rng
    for (n in 1:N) {
        vector[N] gamma_temp;
        if (is_inf(phi)) gamma_temp[n] <- nu[n];
        else gamma_temp[n] <- gamma_rng(phi, phi / nu[n]);
        if (gamma_temp[n] < pow(2.0,30.0))
            y_predict[n] <-  poisson_rng(gamma_temp[n]);
        else y_predict[n] <-  normal_rng(gamma_temp[n], sqrt(gamma_temp[n]));
       }
    }
}

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Ragged negative binomial time series - how to speed up
parts:
You can make this more efficient.

#1 Use the non-centered parameterizations for the hierarchical components.

> beta_seasonal ~ normal(mu_seasonal,sigma_seasonal);

beta_raw is a parameter, beta a transformed parameter (or local variable in model block):

beta_raw ~ normal(0, 1);

beta <- beta_raw * sigma_seasonal + mu_seasonal;

#2 Vectorize wherever possible.

> for(j in 1:J){
>
> // trend evolution
> date_deltas[j_start[j]] ~ normal(0,10); // first observation has looser prior
> for(t in (j_start[j]+1):(j_end[j]-1))
> date_deltas[t] ~ normal(date_deltas[t-1],sigma_delta);

becomes

date_deltas[j_start] ~ normal(0, 10);

for (j in 1:J)
data_deltas[j_start[j] + 1 : j_end[j] - 1]
~ normal(date_deltas[j_start[j] : j_end[j] - 2], sigma_delta);

You'll want to check that indexing.

then you want to collect up all the neg_binomial_2. That might be as
easy as converting this

to

y_data ~ neg_binomial_2_log(y_hat, phi);

If the iteration over j_start/j_end just walks over the whole vector.

The ~ notation will also drop constants, which can be a bit faster.

#3 Munge the indexes so you don't need all the +1 and -1 business.
Usually you can get away with only one array because usually the next
one starts right after the last one ended.

#4 All those cumulative sum calcs are going to be expensive. I don't
see a way to make them cheaper if that's really what you need. Same
thing for the CDFs.

#5 Sorry about making you do this in generated quantities to avoid
rejections; what you have is a nice workaround:

> if (is_inf(phi)) gamma_temp[n] <- nu[n];
> else gamma_temp[n] <- gamma_rng(phi, phi / nu[n]);

same with the overflow. But seriously, if you have problems with this
during sampling (not warmup), you may need a stronger prior on phi
to keep it away from +inf. Also, if the Poisson's overflowing in its RNG,
you have data on a huge scale that's probably also going to be a problem.

- Bob

2/ i haven't changed the generated quantities block yet.  Would you expect that to offer a speed advantage or just tidier code/more disciplined model/priors?

thanks again.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Ragged negative binomial time series - how to speed up
parts:
You can always do the vectorization. How much you save in
time depends on a few things about the distribution like how
many shared subexxpressions there are.

I was trying to balance readability and clarity with efficiency
in the manual, but we've been moving toward the latter.

Generated quantities usually execute much faster because there
are no derivatives.

- Bob

>> You can make this more efficient.
>>
>> #1 Use the non-centered parameterizations for the hierarchical components.
>>
>> > beta_seasonal ~ normal(mu_seasonal,sigma_seasonal);
>>
>> beta_raw is a parameter, beta a transformed parameter (or local variable in model block):
>>
>> beta_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
>>
>> beta <- beta_raw * sigma_seasonal + mu_seasonal;
>>
>> #2 Vectorize wherever possible.
>>
>> > for(j in 1:J){
>> >
>> > // trend evolution
>> > date_deltas[j_start[j]] ~ normal(0,10); // first observation has looser prior
>> > for(t in (j_start[j]+1):(j_end[j]-1))
>> > date_deltas[t] ~ normal(date_deltas[t-1],sigma_delta);
>>
>> becomes
>>
>> date_deltas[j_start] ~ normal(0, 10);
>>
>> for (j in 1:J)
>> data_deltas[j_start[j] + 1 : j_end[j] - 1]
>> ~ normal(date_deltas[j_start[j] : j_end[j] - 2], sigma_delta);
>>
>> You'll want to check that indexing.
>>
>> then you want to collect up all the neg_binomial_2. That might be as
>> easy as converting this
>>
>> > increment_log_prob(neg_binomial_2_log_log(
>> > y_data[j_start[j]:j_end[j]],
>> > y_hat[j_start[j]:j_end[j]],
>> > phi));
>>
>> to
>>
>> y_data ~ neg_binomial_2_log(y_hat, phi);
>>
>> If the iteration over j_start/j_end just walks over the whole vector.
>>
>> The ~ notation will also drop constants, which can be a bit faster.
>>
>> #3 Munge the indexes so you don't need all the +1 and -1 business.
>> Usually you can get away with only one array because usually the next
>> one starts right after the last one ended.
>>
>> #4 All those cumulative sum calcs are going to be expensive. I don't
>> see a way to make them cheaper if that's really what you need. Same
>> thing for the CDFs.
>>
>> #5 Sorry about making you do this in generated quantities to avoid
>> rejections; what you have is a nice workaround:
>>
>> > if (is_inf(phi)) gamma_temp[n] <- nu[n];
>> > else gamma_temp[n] <- gamma_rng(phi, phi / nu[n]);
>>
>> same with the overflow. But seriously, if you have problems with this
>> during sampling (not warmup), you may need a stronger prior on phi
>> to keep it away from +inf. Also, if the Poisson's overflowing in its RNG,
>> you have data on a huge scale that's probably also going to be a problem.
>>
